This question is as important as the question of the world’s coming into being. For religious thinkers, proving that God exists—the foundation of all other questions—depends on it, because they make a thing’s need for a cause depend on its having begun. People who rely on outward appearances are shown only arguments such as “the world is a building, so it must have an ancient builder.” The world’s end, its destruction, and the Last Judgment also depend on its having begun: what is eternal cannot cease to exist. That is why careful philosophers and religious scholars devote so much effort to proving that the world began. But the sound view must bring together religious teaching and proof, while affirming that God’s giving never stops. Among His beautiful names are “the One whose kindness is eternal” and “the One whose hands are open to give.” His words never run out, His light never sets. In short, God’s way of acting cannot be suspended. This can be understood through temporal coming-into-being, inner renewal, and substantial motion, as the author says; or through the “everlasting” coming-into-being taught by the learned Sayyid Dāmād, as we have explained elsewhere. It cannot be understood as the coming-into-being in imaginary time taught by al-Ashʿarī and others, because that would make an effect lag behind its complete cause and would imply that God waits for a certain state, time, or benefit, contrary to the unceasing giving just described. Another account of temporal coming-into-being that brings together religious and philosophical views occurred to me: the world reported by the one who knows it comes into being when that knower does, and passes away when he does. As the Persian verse says: “When a person lays his head down to sleep, / the ropes of his tent come loose.” It is established that matter is not directly perceived in itself. What is directly perceived is something whose existence is also its existence for the one perceiving it. The heavens, earth, and all that lies between them, as pointed to by sense, imagination, or limited intellect, are new. As worldly natural things, all will pass away: the sky will split, the stars scatter, and the sun darken, as happens at death. Take care: this is a subtle point. — س قده

If the philosophers had said that the world is eternal, they were looking at God and His qualities, and at existence itself: the light that drives nonexistence away and illuminates the natures of the heavens, earth, and all that lies between. The world, in this view, is only the “thingness” of natures, and these fade into the reality of existence as a shadow disappears in sunlight. Existence belongs first and truly to God, as ʿAlī says: “I saw nothing without seeing God before it.” A Persian verse says: “A heart lit by knowledge and purity / sees God first in everything it sees.” Even when the limited mind attributes existence to particular natures, it must set aside those relations. In the mystics’ vision, the world is filled with God’s splendor, or else has faded away into Him. They see only God, His qualities, and what belongs to His realm, which are eternal. This does not conflict with saying that natures, considered in their changing natural existence, come into being. — س قده

The point is that motion is the renewal of a thing, and renewal itself is not an independently existing thing. What exists in its own right is the thing being renewed, such as a changing nature or an accident that changes with that nature. Motion itself is like a grammatical particle: it is not a separate thing. This claim is like saying that coming-to-be is not itself something that comes to be, and that being affected is not itself another affected thing. Otherwise, there would be a motion within motion, a coming-to-be of coming-to-be, and an endless chain. There is no motion of motion; a thing moves. — س قده
This discussion was already given in the first journey, in the section on motion. It was also shown there that substantial motion is itself motion and is moved. Keep this in mind. — T. M. (editor).

It is too strong to reject the claim entirely. It may be correct if it means that natures are always coming into being and renewing themselves. Their substantial motion is like the circular motion of the heavens, not like straight motion from one place to another that begins at rest and ends at rest. — س قده
He means that the idea is being taken in place of the actual thing. — T. M. (editor).

The whole collection is denied eternity because, in the author’s view, it has no existence outside the existence of its individual members. A positive claim needs an existing subject. This differs from a universal nature: although it is denied eternity, it can be said to have begun, because it exists through its individual examples. So one can positively say that a collection has begun only if one believes that the collection itself exists over and above its members. The author denies that view. — س قده

“The whole” here means a collection taken as one thing. This does not conflict with the earlier claim that all the individual events began, since that claim treated them one by one, not as one collection. — T. M. (editor).

This is like saying that each person is one, or that one loaf of bread can satisfy someone. We cannot always move from a claim about each individual to a claim about the whole collection, though it sometimes works for a particular purpose. For example, each possible thing is possible; if an infinite collection of possible things existed as one thing, that collection too would be possible. The claim that each event began works in the same way. — س قده
Just as substantial motion is the source of temporal coming-into-being, it is also a higher, “throne-like” source for it. — س قده

Size is necessary because the difference between a natural body and a mathematical body is only whether its dimensions are left open or made definite. Position is necessary because, when a body exists as a body—not as a point or a nonbodily thing—it can have lines meeting at right angles. Its parts then stand in an order. This gives rise to the category of position: the relation of the body’s parts to one another and of the whole to what lies outside it. As for place, if it means distance, the point is clear. If it means surface, it means here the natural region occupied by a body. The philosophers in Aristotle’s school say every body has a natural place, which is its position and ordering; the argument would not apply to the outermost sphere, which has no natural place. Time might seem to beg the question, but it does not: what is required here is the category “when,” not time itself. — س قده

By “fixed in existence,” he means a broader sense than simple existence, broad enough to include things in space. This supports his point that places and regions do not differ in relation to such a thing. — س قده

“The form of change” can mean the change of the form, making the phrase a description of what changes. Or it can mean that substantial motion is the form underlying accidental motions, making it the form belonging to those changes. — س قده
Primordial matter cannot exist apart from form, because matter and form are inseparable and God’s giving does not stop, either at the beginning or at the end. — س قده
The second should be put in place of the first, and the first in place of the second, as is clear. — T. M. (editor).

The difference between a nature and matter is that matter’s level is a level of existence: its existence is pure potentiality. A nature’s level, considered apart from opposite qualities, is only what that nature is. In the upward order of beings, matter is the level that can receive every form and is the material source of the natural world, though it has no actual quality—not even the weakest, which is extension. This is why some say that the beginning of the natural world’s receptive side is darkness, emptiness, or the abyss; they mean matter. — س قده

By “attribute,” the author means an essential feature, like being human for a human being. Change is part of the real existence of bodies. By “what makes the body up,” he means an inner constituent: change is the very existence of the body’s specific form, one of its parts alongside matter and bodily form. Or the phrase means that change is the basis of the qualities that necessarily follow from a kind of thing; the source of a thing’s effects is part of what makes it what it is. The phrase “or part of the level of its existence” means that change or motion goes with a body’s existence and identity and does not come after them, even though it is not part of the abstract definition of the body. In the first two cases, the feature has some kind of priority over the thing; here it does not. — س قده

That is, the motion of the fifth nature belonging to the outermost heaven. Its measure is substantial motion, and both come before positional motion and other accidents. Some things exist along with change and time: the substantial motion of the heavenly natures. Just as the heavens’ positions are always flowing, their natures also flow in their identities. — س قده

Natural natures are inside change and surrounded by time, just as a measured body is contained within its measure. A natural body is contained by its mathematical measure, even though time is also in motion, motion is in a subject, and mathematical measure is in a natural body, as every accident is in its subject. — س قده
He means that the body and separate intellect are alike in one respect, but not in another. The body’s being “with” time is really its being in time, because it undergoes motion. — س قده

No separate thing in the world corresponds to conceptual existence, apart from the actual natures that exist. If existence were a separate thing with its own counterpart, it too would be a basic reality, but that is impossible. — س قده

This explains how they fell into the mistake. They treated existence as a concept in the mind and nature as the true reality. Since the nature of a body, in their view, is free of change and its measure, they said change does not belong to the real nature of bodies. They failed to see that real existence is the luminous, flowing reality of a thing, and that change goes with this existence. They saw change only among the body’s accidents. — س قده

If “belonging to” is a real relation, then in the outer world the subject must already exist before a quality can belong to it. The same is true when a nature is truly said in the mind to have existence: it would have to undergo endless acts of being given existence, just as in the outside world. We cannot treat the mind’s true claim that a nature exists differently from the claim that existence itself exists, unity itself is one, and so on, because in those cases the subject and quality are the same and the mind creates the relation. Here, however, a nature is a different kind of thing from existence, and the relation is assumed to be real. — س قده

There is some imprecision here. Motion is a way of existing and has no separate nature of its own. A better answer is that this view would make a nature itself graded and changeable. — T. M. (editor).

If this argument worked, it would apply to accidental motion. But substantial motion is not a quality that belongs to a subject from outside; the substance itself is moving. So it would not mean that something is a quality of itself. The author’s statements that motion itself does not move and that there is no motion within motion have also been discussed. — T. M. (editor).

The form is the nature that is the body’s first source of activity and motion. It is not pure actuality, but neither is it pure potentiality; it lies between them. The source of actual change cannot be either wholly unchanging or wholly fixed. Also, if the form were unchanging, it would be matter: what would make it deserve the name “form” instead of “matter”? If the point is that the concept of form is not itself changing or fixed, that is what the author is trying to prove. This does not prevent its existence from being changeable. — س قده

Matter is a subject of motion as the bearer of its potentiality; form is a subject as the substantial reality in which motion exists. The whole made of matter and form is also a subject, since it is nothing beyond matter clothed in form. — T. M. (editor).
The wording may be reversed. The intended meaning may be that the form is the predicate and the whole is the subject. — س قده
The whole depends on its members; if the members are new, the whole is even more clearly new. — س قده

The mind’s imagined collection contains only a few individuals and has no meaningful ratio to the infinite collection. A collection conceived by the intellect has one separate, unified existence, like a universal concept, unless it is used to consider the endlessly many individuals as they arise. — س قده

Calling the separate forms “forms of knowledge” may mean that they are God’s active knowledge, or that they are the images of His own detailed knowledge, which is one simple awareness that includes all details. The simple reality contains every existence, and all natures and fixed realities are contained within His names and qualities, like a tree contained in a seed. — س قده

The disagreement here is about coming into being in time, not about depending on a cause in one’s very existence. The theologians excluded time from the events whose beginning they discuss. They did not say that time itself began at a time, since that would require time to exist before time. Instead, they said that it had no limit either in the past or the future. When they were shown that this would make the world eternal, because time is one of the possible things, some said time was only an imagined idea with no reality. That would undermine all their proofs that the world began in time. Others said time is derived from God’s own essence; but that would make God change. They replied that a derived concept can differ in judgment from the thing it comes from. This distinction between a concept and its reality has no clear meaning here; it leads to sophistry. — T. M. (editor).

This does not prove what is needed. The desired conclusion is that events have no first moment in time. What follows is only that an unlimited number of determining causes would exist together at one time. It is better to reject this case because it requires an infinite number of causes confined between two limits: God and the new factor that selects the time. — T. M. (editor).

God is far above additional qualities that come into being, whether the quality itself or its relation to something else is new. Such a change could either make the world new or make God composite, with potentiality and actuality. A new will, for example, would have to be preceded by a readiness to receive it. God is self-sufficient and does not need a condition, a suitable time, an added motive, or anything else. Since He acts by His own essence and by a quality that is His essence, His action never stops. — س قده
That is, His state is always the same: before things exist, while they exist, and afterward. His acts do not change, as God says: “You will find no change in God’s way.” — س قده

You may wonder how this exception connects to the preceding point. Some theologians did not say that causality and agency are identical with God’s essence, which would make the argument for the world’s eternity even stronger. They instead attributed additional qualities to God. But once they accept causes and effects and say that God’s eternal will causes the world, they must identify a factor that explains why the world began at a particular time. — س قده

Put another way: what benefit is there in nonexistence, which is pure evil, instead of existence, which is pure good? Why hold back from giving when a possible nature needs only its own possibility to receive existence, that possibility is eternal, and the source is pure generosity and completely self-sufficient? God’s knowledge of what is beneficial is active, so it cannot be delayed. Also, if God acts to gain a benefit, He is being driven by a motive beyond His essence. — س قده
At the very least, the proposed selector must be something different from the time it selects. — س قده

You might object that this does not apply only to the Karrāmiyya; it also applies to those who say God has additional qualities. The author has not said that it applies only to the Karrāmiyya. Also, he may not have mentioned it earlier because there was no new thing being received in those other cases, so one might deny that they involve a new receptive state. — T. M. (editor).

The same place must contain both the wills and the motions caused by them. This resembles our own voluntary actions: each step results from a particular will, and each such will results in a step. — س قده

This resembles the view that God’s knowledge of things apart from Himself consists of forms in an intellect or soul, rather than in His essence, to avoid the problems discussed earlier. That view would make God depend on something else for His perfection, as this account of will does. — س قده
The same view was quoted earlier, in the general discussion of final causes: it says that will selects a time by its own nature. Remember what we explained there. — س قده

He says this because philosophical conclusions must be proved. The philosophers who spoke this way seem to have been arguing against a theologian by accepting the theologian’s own starting point. — س قده

This is the view that God eternally willed the world to exist at a future time. Its supporter imagines time as outside the chain of possible things: an endless stretch with a past and a future, over which God’s existence extends forever. God, existing in eternity, willed the world to exist in the future. The author rejects this by pointing out that time is the measure of motion—either the motion of universal nature, in his view, or the motion of the outermost sphere, in another account. In either case, time is possible. If all possible things are set aside, only sheer nonexistence remains. There is no time there with separate moments to which an eternal will could be attached differently. — T. M. (editor).
It would be more accurate to say “later” or “afterward.” Our will is mixed with potentiality; God’s will is not. — س قده
By “the time before it” or “another time,” he means other possible instances of time. They do not exist outside the mind, but the mind can picture them. — س قده

The point is that God’s giving to the natural world never stops, even though its parts are continually renewed through substantial motion. This can be true even if some universal kinds endure: according to ancient science, the heavens, stars, the four elements, and composite kinds such as human beings, animals, and plants continue because their individuals replace one another. The argument uses old ideas about astronomy and the order of nature, including the belief that the heavens and their motions last forever and that the four elements are always present beneath the moon. These assumptions have since been disproved by precise experiments: Earth and the other three bodies once called elements are mixtures of different elements; heavenly bodies are also composite and have limited, though long, lifetimes; and the time once measured by the daily movement of the outermost sphere is measured instead by Earth’s rotation and yearly movement around the sun. Still, the author’s argument holds if we replace those old assumptions with modern ones. The world’s nature, through its continuing substantial change, exists in a flowing time and must come into being again and again. There is no problem in saying that God’s giving never ends while forms change, kinds disappear, or a new world arises as the forms of another pass away. The divine outpouring never stops. Several reports from the Imams of the Prophet’s family support this: God has always created one creation after another, one world after another, and will continue to do so. No natural kind that exists in time is eternal and without a first moment. First matter and the universal nature that underlies particular kinds are both indeterminate; temporal kinds give them their specific form. Separate, immaterial beings exist outside time and are not spread across it. It is a mistake to imagine that God, or any immaterial being, exists stretched across an endless span of time. — T. M. (editor).

This alludes to the verse: “The Jews say, ‘God’s hand is tied up.’ May their hands be tied, and may they be cursed for what they say. Rather, both His hands are open; He gives as He wills.” The author suggests that those who say God withholds His giving resemble the Jews in this respect. His point is that a careful philosopher must affirm God’s eternity and the eternity of what belongs to Him, while also affirming that creation begins from its own side. — س قده

That is, the sphere of fire, the sphere of air, and so on. Each sphere is one continuous body, so each kind persists as a single individual. Fire and air themselves, along with the other elements, are kinds with many separate individuals. — س قده

Every one of these arguments assumes that time lies outside the realm of possible things. Time must then either be an imagined construct or something drawn from God’s own being and identical with Him—which is impossible. — T. M. (editor).

The copies consulted here have a line missing: “If that is impossible, the events end at nonexistence; if it is possible …” The point is that neither option gives an infinite series of events. The argument asks whether events fail to reach back into eternity or are found there. A kind exists if at least one of its individuals exists, and ceases only if all its individuals cease. If no event exists in eternity, the series is finite because it ends in nonexistence. If one does exist there, that event is the beginning of the series that continues without end into the future; the series is still finite on that side because it begins with that one event. — س قده

A better reply is this: for something to be absent is for its existence to be removed. Its eternal nonexistence is not such a removal, because it could not have existed in eternity and was not meant to exist forever. Its genuine absence is the absence that stands opposite to its existence at the time when it exists. That existence has displaced absence and does not itself admit of nonexistence. What admits of existence or nonexistence is its essence, which in itself has no existence; this is absence that accompanies the thing. By contrast, absence in the past would imply an earlier existence in time. If there was no earlier temporal existence, there was no earlier temporal absence. Necessary existence is neither temporal nor opposed to existence in this way. Also, absence is pure negation, so it cannot be treated as something that is “eternal,” nor can all absences be gathered together in eternity. — س قده

If someone says that past events are infinite, how can they also accept that each event’s absence is not preceded by an event? If this means that an absence does not coexist with any event, that is denied. “Preceded” and “followed” here refer to the ends of periods of absence, not to their beginnings, which coincide with the events in question. — س قده
Put more clearly: an absence is not paired with a particular event—either the event whose absence it is, or a later event in the endless future. — س قده

Eternity, too, is a negative idea: it is like a container with no beginning. Something eternal is simply something that exists in, or belongs to, what has no beginning. So there is no contradiction in saying that both a thing’s existence and its absence are eternal in this sense: both fall within what has no beginning. A further reply is that eternity is not a fixed time or a particular instant that can hold only one thing. It can contain a thing and its removal at different levels, just as the past can contain both Noah’s existence and his absence. More fully, this uses the familiar theologians’ sense of “eternal” as what lies at the beginning of the descending chain from the hidden depths of reality to the visible world, and “everlasting” as what lies at the far end of the ascending chain from outward things to their inner realities. There is also a deeper sense: eternal reality is existence before it is linked to any particular form in any realm, while everlasting reality is that same existence after all forms have been erased by the overpowering One. Once this is understood, there is no conflict between absences in eternity and an endless succession of events in the past, just as all things may come to an end in everlastingness while events continue without end into the future. Their absence is their return to God along the vertical chain of being. Their source lies in the descending chain; their return lies in the ascending chain. Endless changes and stages may unfold across time, with endless relations and destinations, yet all rise along that chain to God, the final end and goal: “To your Lord is the return, and to Him is the end.” — س قده
Eternity is not a fixed boundary or a measured time. It is as explained above. — س قده
This refers to the earlier claim that the philosophers’ famous doctrine—that kinds are eternal and their essences are preserved through successive individuals—is mistaken. — س قده
Perhaps the reason is that a shared universal is abstract and exists only through its individual instances. — T. M. (editor).

The claim is that the whole is not eternal, not that it begins to exist as a separate thing. It has no existence apart from its parts, or within any one part. A natural universal is different: although it has no existence apart from individuals, it exists through the existence of any one individual. A kind exists when at least one of its individuals exists and ceases only when all of them cease. This is the point the author calls the root of the matter. — س قده

Some theologians say that God is not the complete cause of the world’s existence, in order to avoid saying that the world is eternal. They fail to see that the natural world is originated in its very being, even though God is a complete and more-than-complete cause: necessary in Himself and necessary in every respect. Nothing in Him is other than His own pure being. What they say amounts to claiming that God is not rich and sufficient to create the world, but needs something else to become an active cause—even if that means waiting through an endless number of measured periods. They have wrongly compared the whole to one of its parts. A person such as Zayd depends on causes, conditions, and preparations outside himself, so God is not the complete cause of Zayd if the question is only about Zayd’s own power. Yet God needs nothing else to create Zayd: He creates everything on which Zayd’s existence depends. Nothing possible lies outside the world; everything on which the world depends, other than God, belongs to it. So the world depends only on God and His attributes, which are identical with His essence. To ask whether God’s essence is enough to create the whole world, or whether He needs something besides Himself, leaves only two possible answers. To choose the second is an outrageous denial of His self-sufficiency. How can cause and effect be equal in rank? As the author has said repeatedly, the world’s coming to be is essential, not temporal. — س قده

The whole is made up of infinitely many groups, each group being like one individual event. The fact that each individual event begins does not prove that the whole series is finite; the same is true of the series of groups. — س قده

The difference is that each group of souls consists of parts existing together, while each group of events consists of parts occurring one after another. This is another account of the world’s coming to be. As Shaykh Mahmud Shabistari writes in the Gulshan-i Raz: “The whole world, at every moment, becomes nothing, and does not remain for two moments.” — س قده
Perhaps this argument appears in the Matarihat in the form of a question beginning “I say …”; the author therefore calls it a question. — س قده

“In an unusual arrangement.” Even if such an arrangement is rare, that would not make the number of souls finite. It could recur endlessly over endlessly many cycles and revolutions. A rare alignment in one cycle could occur again in other cycles—for example, at the midpoint of another revolution of the sphere of fixed stars. — س قده

The author gives four replies. First, divine providence would not allow this kind, the noblest of natural kinds, to disappear when less noble kinds exist from eternity. But providence also takes account of the conditions, causes, and preparations required for other things. It is possible that this kind’s conditions were present for a limited period: it appeared, its individuals lived in succession, it disappeared, and the conditions later returned so that it appeared again. The kind may exist for longer than it is absent, with providence giving each thing its due. The claim that less noble kinds exist forever seems to refer to the four elements and the heavenly bodies, whose supposed eternity has already been challenged. Second, the rule of “the possibility of the nobler” is applied to kinds in general; but that rule depends on proving that the less noble kinds exist, which has not been done. Third, the existence of luminous archetypes that care for their material kinds would mean that no kind is ever absent from existence. But even if such archetypes exist, they are not complete causes: their effects still depend on conditions and readiness. As explained above, these may be present only at some times, not all the time, and may operate intermittently. The author has already discussed the archetypes in the first journey’s treatment of essences. Fourth, some mystics call this form a divine name or a manifestation of the First Reality. But it is not a universal divine name; it is a name belonging to the world. Such worldly names need not persist forever. The same applies to manifestations. — T. M. (editor).
The lower world is a shadow of the higher one. Since every active intellect is everlasting, each intelligible form there must have an everlasting shadow here. — س قده

The author did not conclude that number is eternal. He concluded that multiplicity, which belongs to the category of number, is only a mental construct. This is also the mystics’ view: number is the mind’s repetition of “one” without specifying what kind of one it is, and repeating something in thought does not multiply the thing itself. — س قده

“They look united, but their hearts are divided.” These souls do not form one whole with the first, nearest beings, because they have no shared nature with them. This echoes the earlier point in the Matarihat that separate souls do not form a whole, since no relation binds them together. — س قده
This qualification is needed if the argument is a reductio; it is not needed if it is offered as a direct proof. — س قده
This is like the argument about the last effect before the final cause. — س قده

You may think this conflicts with the earlier reply to the “divine philosopher,” where the author says that number exists. His point there is that numbers exist as many repeated units. Here he is describing the opponent’s view: that number has no existence at all, because the unit from which number is formed is only a mental construct for him. This reading is supported by the author’s description of number as a weakly existing essence whose form is its own matter. — س قده

The act of causing takes place at the instant that separates a period of existence from a period of nonexistence. This is the boundary where something begins to exist: coming to be is existence after nonexistence, just as persistence is existence after existence. The cause acts on existence marked by its coming after nonexistence, at the first instant, not at a second instant; otherwise it would be producing something that already exists. If the effect did not begin in time, there would be no act of causing it. The author discussed this point near the beginning of the first journey. — س قده
This argument seems stronger because it establishes an intermediate state between existence and nonexistence. — T. M. (editor).
Composite making cannot apply to essential attributes. — س قده
That is, the effect depends on its agent for its very existence, and the agent acts through its own essential powers. — س قده

This may be inferred from the wording of their argument. But since they do not accept continuous substantial motion, their claim that like things replace one another would mean that the body has a different individual essence at every instant from the body in the preceding instant. Common sense rules that out. — T. M. (editor).

There would be no persistence from one instant to the next. But instantaneous states and a series of separate instants are impossible. The truth is continuous renewal through substantial motion, as explained above. — س قده

The fact that something could cease to exist does not mean it did not exist eternally in time. A universal intellect, for example, could possibly cease to exist and yet have existed forever in time. More briefly, one could use the same reply given for motion: if rest is a thing’s second state of being in one place, it must have been preceded by its first state there. — س قده
This follows from treating what distinguishes one thing as its defining feature: a distinguishing feature presupposes something shared in essence. — س قده

Since coming to be is continual renewal in a thing’s very being, persistence is stability. But a state “between” two limits cannot be stable: at every instant it lies between two boundaries different from those of the instant before and the instant after. It is like a point that keeps moving, held in a continually passing present. — س قده
This follows the author’s account of composition as a unity of matter and form. — س قده
In debate, showing that the opponent’s reason for denying a claim does not hold does not by itself prove the claim. The opponent may still ask for evidence. — T. M. (editor).

The middle term in this proof is expressly qualified as “in itself.” It therefore applies to substantial motion and yields the world’s temporal beginning as the author has explained it. The theologians do not make this qualification. They argue that a body is never free of events, and that whatever is never free of events must have begun. Their smaller and larger premises are both unsound. The same problem affects their argument that the world changes and everything that changes must have begun. If they had limited change to what occurs in a thing’s very being, the argument would be valid. — T. M. (editor).
That is, the thing’s substance and nature continually flow because of substantial motion. — س قده
Eternity is not a fixed span of time, as explained above. — س قده
A negative statement can be true because there is no subject for it to describe. Eternity is not a particular time. — س قده
That is, a motion so called, or what they call “motion in the middle.” Otherwise, each instance of motion would itself be preceded by another instance. — س قده

Reward and punishment may be understood as a vertical return to God, so people should not imagine that saying the world is eternal denies the afterlife. Yet the claim still causes a problem: if the world never comes to an end, people do not understand the afterlife or the ascending and descending chains of being, whose final goal is reached by turning toward inner, higher worlds. Even if that account is accepted, it still weakens the proof of the Creator, since people take the world’s coming to be as the reason it needs a cause. — س قده
Or one may suppose an endless number of imagined or estimated periods, simply to show that nothing prevents God’s wisdom from acting; nothing can obstruct His judgment. — س قده

“Existent” here means existent in the everyday sense: a thing’s essence or what-it-is, not existence itself. Sameness and difference belong to essences. In this sense, the world is the realm of essences. — س قده

The word “dominant” can be used broadly, and what counts as dominant depends on how the speaker is looking at things, as in the phrase “the sun and the moon.” For separate beings, time is eternity, or dahr. If someone says that the intellects are eternal in time, “time” here means dahr, as explained earlier. Dahr is the spirit of time, just as everlastingness is the spirit of dahr. One may also speak of their time as the time their existence would have, if it were measured; that is enough for this way of speaking. — س قده

The author’s words do not mean that bodies existed before time. Nor does the phrase “bodies are eternal in time” necessarily mean that time preceded them. The preposition “in” can indicate the aspect under discussion, as in the expressions “a human being is material in body, immaterial in spirit, actual in existence, and potential in essence.” The intended meaning is that bodies’ existence is temporal, or that they exist along with time. — س قده

The mystic did not speak of time and bodies existing together; he spoke of time preceding them. The reply is that the author hints that the mystic’s wording does not establish such temporal priority. At most, it says they exist together, which does not conflict with the essential priority that the mystic himself accepts. — س قده

There is no temporal simultaneity here, as between two separate things. Time and what exists in time are bound together, like matter and form. Just as, on the author’s view, one cannot say that form is eternal merely because matter is, as if they were two separate things existing alongside each other, one cannot speak of time and temporal things as two separate things existing together. Their connection has been explained above. — س قده

This is a good reading of the mystic’s words. But it leaves a problem: given the dependence between them, it either denies priority in either direction between bodies and time, or gives each priority over the other—bodies because they cause time to exist, and time because it gives bodies their particular form. Yet the mystic denies priority to time and grants it only to bodies. — T. M. (editor).

As noted in the first journey’s discussion of time, each motion has its own duration: the stretch that belongs to it and is measured by it. There are therefore as many durations as there are motions. The familiar time measured by the daily motion of the heavens is an agreed standard for measuring other motions. Saying that this familiar time makes a thing distinct means that it reveals its distinctness. The time of a body’s movement through one of its accidental features comes only after the body exists and is already distinct. If a body has a time that makes it distinct, that time is the measure of its own substantial motion, which is its flowing existence. — T. M. (editor).

This follows from the meaning of necessary existence in itself. Anything necessary in itself must exist under every supposition: whether anything else exists or does not exist. Suppose we consider time and set everything else aside. Everything else is then removed, leaving only time itself. Yet the Necessary Being is not removed; He exists even under the supposition that time alone exists. So God is with every thing, without being joined to it. — T. M. (editor).
